channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Researchers show a coin-sized implant can manipulate 737 NG flight management data over ARINC 429
item.description: A team from the University of California San Diego and Oberlin College has demonstrated that a hardware implant roughly the size of a coin, costing under 100 dollars to build, can interfere with communications between key Boeing 737 NG avionics. The device attaches to a maintenance connection in the electronics bay beneath the cockpit, reachable in about fifteen seconds with no special tools through an exterior hatch that maintenance and ground staff routinely access. Rather than breaking into a computer, it injects electrical signals onto the ARINC 429 data bus, overpowering legitimate traffic to substitute manipulated information. In the laboratory the team altered a flight plan and manipulated weight and performance data, and explored concealing changes from the pilot display. The work was done on a bench-built avionics testbed, not an operational aircraft. - USENIX Security research, UC San Diego and Oberlin College — reported by Aerospace Global News - Presented Aug 2026; reported 19 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Ransomware took out door access, elevators and HVAC monitoring at a major hospital — a week later they were still restoring it
item.description: Shared Health confirmed that ransomware discovered on 10 August at Winnipeg’s Health Sciences Centre, Manitoba’s largest hospital, disrupted building systems as well as clinical IT. Electronic door access, elevator control and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning monitoring were affected, and staff reverted to manual processes; a recovery update on 17 August confirmed restoration was still under way. This is not an aviation incident, and it is included because the affected systems are the ones an airport terminal depends on and manages the same way. Access control, lifts, escalators, baggage-hall HVAC and terminal BMS typically sit on shared IT infrastructure, are administered by facilities or a building-services contractor, and are not in the airport’s security-programme asset inventory until something like this happens. - Shared Health statements — reported by CBC News; supporting building-systems exposure data from Claroty Team82 - Attack discovered 10 Aug 2026; Shared Health recovery update 17 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Clop names more than 40 PTC Windchill victims, with aerospace among the confirmed sectors
item.description: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations on its leak site following a mass data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management platforms, exploiting CVE-2026-12569, an improper input validation flaw allowing arbitrary code execution. Named organisations include Shell, Philips, Fiserv, Zebra, Mindray and Largan Precision. Researchers report affiliates deploying JSP web shells to exfiltrate data, with confirmed victims across manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and retail, and activity running since early June. What was taken is specific: engineering blueprints, product designs and manufacturing specifications. For airlines, MRO providers and airport engineering teams, the exposure runs through the supply chain — component design data, repair procedures and configuration records for aircraft systems and ground support equipment sit in exactly these platforms at tier-one and tier-two suppliers, and the published victim list is not a complete one. - Clop leak-site listings — reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Listings reported 15 Aug 2026; campaign since early Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers, commercial facilities in scope
item.description: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build custom tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software, providing read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over S7comm. Critical manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities are named as most targeted. Actors find exposed devices using internet scanning services and gain access through default or weakly configured credentials rather than a vulnerability. Affected lines span S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 including F-series safety controllers. Airports sit inside the commercial facilities scope through their ground OT: baggage handling and sortation, jet bridges, fuelling and hydrant systems, de-icing, airfield lighting, and terminal building management — much of it installed by systems integrators with remote support connectivity the airport did not arrange itself. - Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Issued 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Industrial ransomware rose 12 percent in Q2 and disrupted operations without touching control systems
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first quarter, with manufacturing accounting for 747, construction 176, equipment manufacturing 114 and food and beverage 70. The finding that carries into aviation is mechanical rather than sectoral: disrupting the IT systems supporting an operation is frequently enough to interrupt it even where attackers never reach a control system, and extortion continued shifting from encryption toward data theft. Aviation has already lived this pattern through shared passenger-processing platforms, where an attack on a single supplier forced manual check-in and baggage handling across multiple large European hubs. The systems that stop an airport are rarely the ones controlling machinery — they are the ones that tell the machinery what to do and record that it was done. - Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Claroty finds one in five facility cyber-physical assets a single hop from internet-exposed systems
item.description: Team82 analysed more than 750,000 cyber-physical assets across large facilities and found nearly one in five sitting one hop from a system making outbound internet connections. Close to 90 percent of the building management systems examined communicated over insecure protocols and 40 percent ran outdated firmware, with around a third of HVAC and cooling systems one hop from an internet-exposed system. The study covers data centres, but the asset classes are the same as a terminal building: power distribution, building management, physical access control, fire protection and cooling. At an airport those systems are usually owned by property or facilities rather than by an OT team, procured under concession or capital contracts, and connected by suppliers for remote monitoring — and physical access control in particular is a security-restricted-area control that regulators care about, not simply a building service. - Claroty Team82, State of CPS Security: Data Center Exposures — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 29 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
item.description: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. At an airport NetScaler commonly fronts remote access for ground-handling, baggage-system, BMS and airfield lighting vendors, and for airlines it fronts crew, ops and MRO application access. An unauthenticated bypass on that appliance defeats the boundary that most airport security programmes are relying on to keep vendor access controlled. - Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. CISA names transportation systems and commercial facilities among the affected sectors, and terminals are exactly that. Airport fire detection is managed from workstations that sit with facilities or a building-services contractor, are often physically accessible in back-of-house areas, and rarely appear in the airport security programme asset inventory. That is the local access this flaw needs. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28 - Published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers are exploiting to force appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition, requiring no authentication and no user interaction. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. In aviation these appliances commonly terminate supplier access into baggage, fuelling and building systems, connect outstations and remote airfield facilities, and carry airline access into airport-hosted systems — so an unexpected reload removes remote support at exactly the wrong moment during a disruption. - Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek - Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] August ICS Patch Tuesday: critical code execution in Siveillance VMS, maximum severity in IoT2050
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. A critical code execution vulnerability was fixed in Siveillance Video Management Servers, and SSA-834709 covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices allowing a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code with elevated privileges. High-severity flaws were addressed in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort, with medium-severity issues resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published advisories covering NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact one covering multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Honeywell released several advisories for its building management products. Siveillance and Desigo are the items most likely to be in an airport estate, covering terminal and airfield video surveillance and terminal building services respectively. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709 and related Siemens, Schneider, Phoenix Contact and Honeywell advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Johnson Controls Airwall arbitrary file read in CISA’s mid-August advisory batch
item.description: CISA’s advisories published in the 11 to 13 August window included Johnson Controls Airwall, ICSA-26-225-03, with an arbitrary file read vulnerability; Johnson Controls recommends applying version 4.1.0 or later to all Airwall deployments. The same batch covered Hitachi Energy APM Edge, ICSA-26-225-04, where CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500 let a local unprivileged user escalate to root in versions up to and including 6.10, and ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA. Airwall is the one most likely to appear in an airport estate, since it is frequently deployed as the secure overlay providing remote connectivity to distributed building, access control and baggage systems, and to give vendors scoped remote support. A file-read flaw in the product mediating that access warrants more than routine advisory handling, because it sits on the boundary the rest of the architecture depends on. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-225-03 and ICSA-26-225-04 - Published 11–13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two further additions followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. For airports and airlines the IKE and vCenter entries carry the most weight. IKE terminates the site-to-site tunnels connecting terminals, outstations, cargo facilities and supplier networks. vCenter frequently manages the virtual infrastructure hosting airport operational databases, baggage reconciliation, resource management and flight information display systems, where a compromise is a hypervisor-level problem affecting every workload at once. SharePoint deserves a second look because airport security programmes, restricted-area drawings and standard operating procedures are commonly stored there. - CISA KEV catalogue additions - Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT monitoring suite
item.description: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments, which could let an attacker cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code. Affected versions are below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02, a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can lead to remote code execution if a user is tricked into running the affected binary with a malicious string; Siemens has released fixed versions. Malcolm appears in airport environments more often than its profile suggests, usually stood up by an airport IT or facilities team to get visibility into baggage and building networks without a commercial OT monitoring budget — placed on a span port with sight of the whole ground-systems network, and rarely in a patch inventory. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02 - Published 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] A low-privilege Metasys user can plant a payload that runs in an administrator’s browser
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-14, published 13 August, describes a stored cross-site scripting flaw in Johnson Controls Metasys. A user with low privileges can inject a payload through a crafted URL; the payload persists across logins and then executes in the browser context of anyone who subsequently views it, administrators included. Metasys 12, 13, 14 and 15 are affected. That is a privilege-escalation path inside the building management platform rather than a remote takeover, and there is no report of exploitation. Metasys is one of the most widely deployed building management platforms in terminal buildings, cargo sheds and airport office estates, where it drives HVAC, lighting, and in many installations feeds into access control. The flaw is not dramatic on its own, but the Winnipeg hospital ransomware case earlier this month is a reminder of how quickly a building-systems compromise turns into a physical-operations problem — and a persistent payload running with administrator context inside the BMS UI is a serviceable first step. - CISA ICSA-26-225-14 — Johnson Controls product security advisory - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Watchdog finds FAA cybersecurity framework unchanged since 2023 and zero-trust alignment incomplete
item.description: A Government Accountability Office review of aviation cybersecurity, GAO-26-107693, found that the FAA and TSA are collaborating but that key shortfalls remain. Among the specific findings: the FAA has not fully reported its cybersecurity spending or implemented its cybersecurity strategy, its cybersecurity framework has been unchanged since August 2023, and it fully aligns with fewer than half of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s zero-trust migration practices. The GAO also noted that no successful cyberattack against avionics has been reported. For operators the report is context rather than obligation, but it is useful context: it indicates where federal attention is likely to be directed next, and it lands in the same month as research demonstrating a physical-access path into flight management data — a combination that tends to accelerate rulemaking rather than slow it. - US Government Accountability Office, GAO-26-107693 — coverage via ClearanceJobs - Coverage 24 Jul 2026

item.title: [Medium] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations take effect on 11 September 2026. From that date, manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting those products: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a full notification within 72 hours, and a final report within 14 days of a corrective measure being available, or within a month for a severe incident. Reporting flows through a single reporting platform to the relevant national CSIRT, with information made available to ENISA simultaneously. The obligations cover products already on the EU market, not only new releases. For aviation the immediate effect is on the supply side: manufacturers of ground support equipment, baggage systems, passenger processing platforms and building controls sold into the EU acquire a disclosure duty, and airports and airlines buying from them should expect faster, more formal notification from September. - European Commission, Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations - Obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026
